rows.selection_reason: With zero completed experiments, there is no evidence to guide exploitation, so the priority is establishing a clean, interpretable baseline. config_001 (RNA-only, singleprofile, PCA n2000) is the simplest configuration in the design space: a single modality, the simplest profile setting, and a standard linear encoder with no learned parameters. This gives a well-defined reference performance against which all subsequent experiments (multiprofile aggregation, alternative RNA encoders, image-only, and multimodal fusion) can be meaningfully compared. If multimodal or multiprofile models later fail to exceed this simple baseline, that is a critical finding about where added complexity is unhelpful. Starting here minimizes confounding (no aggregation, no fusion, no image) and reduces uncertainty about whether the basic RNA signal is informative at all, making it the most efficient first use of the experiment budget.

With only one completed experiment (config_001: rna_only/singleprofile/pca_n2000, acc≈0.485), the largest source of uncertainty is whether image features carry any useful signal for this task. Testing image_only with a standard resnet50 encoder and singleprofile (config_010) is the cleanest single-variable comparison to the RNA baseline: it isolates the modality question without confounding by aggregation, fusion, or encoder complexity. If image_only performs comparably or better, it justifies investing subsequent budget in multimodal fusion strategies; if it performs poorly, it redirects effort toward improving RNA representations (scvi, scgpt) or multiprofile aggregation. This is the highest-information experiment under the current sparse evidence because it resolves the most fundamental design decision before committing to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: Only two experiments are complete. RNA (pca_n2000, singleprofile) achieves 48.5% acc while image (resnet50, singleprofile) is very weak at 20.8% acc, establishing RNA as the dominant modality. Uncertainty: We have no information on whether the RNA representation itself can be improved—pca_n2000 is a simple linear projection, and it is unclear whether a learned, biologically-informed encoder (scvi_n200) would capture more discriminative structure. This experiment (config_004: rna_only, singleprofile, scvi_n200) changes only the RNA encoder relative to config_001, providing a clean one-variable comparison. It will clarify whether representation quality is a bottleneck: if scvi_n200 substantially improves accuracy, it justifies investing further in learned encoders and multimodal combinations built on them; if it does not, PCA-level representations may suffice and we can redirect budget toward profile setting, aggregation, or fusion. Under a limited budget, resolving this foundational question about the strongest modality's representation is the highest-information next step before committing to more complex multimodal or multiprofile configurations.

Evidence: scvi_n200 (0.520 acc) clearly outperforms pca_n2000 (0.485 acc) in singleprofile RNA-only settings, and image-only resnet50 is very weak (0.208), indicating RNA is the dominant signal. Uncertainty: We have no data yet on whether multiprofile + aggregation improves over singleprofile, and whether the benefit (if any) depends on the RNA encoder. This experiment (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool) directly compares against config_004 (scvi_n200, singleprofile) to isolate the effect of multiprofile with simple average-pool aggregation while holding the encoder fixed. Choosing avgpool over transformer first is the more conservative, interpretable step: if simple averaging does not help, it questions the value of multiprofile broadly; if it does, it motivates testing transformer aggregation next. This is the highest-information single experiment under budget because it extends the best-performing configuration along one new design axis without introducing confounds (no new encoder, no image modality, no fusion).

Evidence: config_005 (RNA-only, multi-profile, scVI_n200, avgpool) achieved 0.650 accuracy, a dramatic ~13-point jump over its single-profile counterpart (config_004, 0.520), establishing that multi-profile representation with scVI is the strongest direction so far. Uncertainty: we do not yet know whether the aggregation method (avgpool vs. transformer) meaningfully affects performance in this multi-profile setting. Question tested: config_006 is identical to config_005 except it replaces avgpool with transformer aggregation, cleanly isolating the effect of the aggregation strategy. Why best next experiment: This is a single-variable, directly comparable follow-up to the best result, so the outcome will tell us whether the simpler avgpool is sufficient or whether a learned transformer aggregation unlocks further gains. That answer will propagate to every subsequent multimodal configuration (configs 018-051 all include an aggregation choice), making this the highest-information-per-experiment choice under the limited budget.

Evidence: Multiprofile with scvi_n200 is the strongest configuration so far (0.650 acc, 0.628 F1), a large jump over singleprofile scvi_n200 (0.520). Aggregation (avgpool vs transformer) shows negligible difference (~0.003). The encoder effect is moderate: scvi_n200 beat pca_n2000 by ~3.5 points in singleprofile. However, scgpt—a fundamentally different pre-trained single-cell model—has not been tested at all. Question: Does scgpt outperform scvi_n200 in the multiprofile setting, or is scvi_n200 the ceiling for RNA encoders? config_008 (scgpt, multiprofile, avgpool) is a clean single-variable comparison against config_005 (scvi_n200, multiprofile, avgpool), isolating the encoder effect in the highest-performing regime. Why this is the best next step: It directly tests whether a different encoder architecture can push beyond the current 0.65 ceiling, using the same profile and aggregation as our best result. If scgpt matches or beats scvi_n200, we gain a new direction; if it underperforms, we confirm scvi_n200 is the best encoder and can redirect budget toward multimodal fusion or other dimensions with greater confidence.

Evidence: RNA-only with scVI n200 and multi-profile achieves ~0.65 accuracy, while image-only with ResNet50 is very weak (0.21). The single image data point (config_010) leaves major uncertainty about whether the image modality can contribute meaningfully. Question: Does a stronger image encoder (ViT-L pretrained on ImageNet) produce a competitive image representation, or is the image modality fundamentally weak for this task? This experiment isolates the image-encoder variable by comparing directly to config_010 (same image-only, single-profile setup, only the encoder changes). Why this is the best next step: Before investing limited budget in complex multimodal fusion configurations (configs 028-051), we need to know whether the image branch can produce a useful signal at all. If ViT-L image-only remains weak (<0.35), multimodal fusion is unlikely to help and we should focus on refining the RNA-only pipeline. If it is competitive (>0.5), multimodal fusion becomes a high-priority direction. This single experiment resolves a critical uncertainty that gates many downstream decisions, making it the most information-dense use of the next budget slot.

Evidence: RNA-only with scvi_n200 + multiprofile + transformer (config_006, acc=0.653) is the clear best configuration, far exceeding image-only models (≤0.227). The multiprofile setting and scvi_n200 encoder are strongly validated. Uncertainty: it is unknown whether adding the image modality (very weak alone) provides complementary signal to the already-strong RNA representation, or whether it introduces noise. This experiment (config_032: multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) is the direct multimodal extension of config_006, changing only the addition of image + concat fusion. This isolates the effect of the image modality against the best known RNA baseline. It is the most informative next step because it answers the central question—does multimodal fusion improve upon the strong RNA-only result—before committing budget to further multimodal variants (weighted fusion, ViT, scgpt). If it fails to beat 0.653, it saves many downstream multimodal experiments; if it succeeds, it justifies exploring fusion type and image encoder.

The best result so far is config_032 (multimodal, multiprofile, scvi_n200, resnet50, transformer, concat) at 0.688 acc, which outperforms the best RNA-only multiprofile (config_006, 0.653 acc) by ~3.5 pp, suggesting the image modality adds modest but real value. However, we have only one multimodal data point and have not yet isolated the effect of the fusion strategy. Config_033 is identical to config_032 except it uses weighted fusion instead of concat, making it a clean single-variable A/B comparison. This tells us whether the way modalities are combined is a meaningful design lever or whether concat is already near-optimal. Under a limited budget, this is the highest-information next step: it either confirms concat is sufficient (freeing us to explore image encoder quality or aggregation next) or reveals that weighted fusion meaningfully improves multimodal performance, guiding subsequent experiments toward better fusion-aware configurations.

Evidence: The current best is config_033 (scvi_n200, resnet50, multiprofile, transformer, weighted) at 0.7131 acc, showing that multimodal fusion with weighted combination provides a substantial boost over RNA-only multiprofile (0.6530). However, the only image encoder tested in multimodal is resnet50, which alone achieves only 0.208 acc. The stronger imagenet_vit_l (0.227 alone) has not been tested in the multimodal setting. Question: Does a higher-capacity image encoder (imagenet_vit_l vs resnet50) improve multimodal fusion performance when all other design choices are held at their best-known values? This is a clean single-variable comparison (image encoder only) against the current best, isolating the effect of image representation quality on fusion. Why best next experiment: Under a limited budget, resolving whether the image modality's contribution is encoder-dependent or encoder-agnostic is critical. If vit_l helps, it justifies further investment in image quality; if it doesn't, it confirms the image signal is inherently limited and we should focus remaining budget on RNA-side or fusion refinements. This single experiment reduces the most important remaining uncertainty about the multimodal architecture.
